warmup.q: An order's life is a switch over a sealed OrderState, with a case for each of its five states and no default. You add a sixth state, WaitingAtShop, for parcels nobody was home to receive. What happens when you build?
options: It compiles; waiting orders go to the first case that matches
It compiles; waiting orders throw MatchException when the switch meets one
It fails to compile at every switch over OrderState that has no default
It fails only if a test calls the switch with a WaitingAtShop value
warmup.why: A switch expression over a sealed type must cover every permitted subtype. With no default to catch the new one, javac reports "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values" at each such switch, and that list of errors is exactly the list of places that need a rule. MatchException only appears when a subtype arrives from code compiled separately, after the switch was compiled.

opening:
An order at the corner shop lives a short life. Someone places it, a packer boxes it in the back room, Pedal Post's rider or a Big Blue Vans driver takes it away, and someone signs for it at the door. The shop's screen has a button for each step: Pack, Ship, Deliver and Cancel. What a button may do depends on where the order is. Cancel is fine while the order sits on the packing table. Once the van has left, it's too late.

Complaints travel too. The shop assistant sorts out what she can, passes bigger ones to the manager, and the manager sends the rest to head office.

The easy trap is to scatter the rules, with an if in every button checking what its author remembered. The last lesson ended by asking how to keep an order's rules in one place. In this lesson, we'll make an order's states and events data, with every rule in one function the compiler checks (State). Then we'll pass a complaint along a line of people until one of them answers (Chain of Responsibility). Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with the buttons on an order screen and a complaint at the counter. The buttons full of ifs became one transition function over sealed states, and the compiler listed every switch a new state touches. The complaint became a chain of handlers, where each one answers or calls next.

Now look in your own code for a status field that several methods compare with if (status == ...). Each of those methods is a button holding part of the rules.

Next, we'll send an inspector through the breakfast box, with a different check for each kind of item. When the kinds stay fixed and the jobs keep growing, where should the new code go?

sections.h: State: an order's life in one function instead of four buttons
sections.html:
The shop's first order screen kept track of an order with a status field: an enum (a type with a fixed list of values) holding PLACED, PACKED, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED or CANCELLED. Each button changes the status, and each one checks what its author remembered:

Java
// Naive: each button guards only what its author thought of
void pack()    { if (status == Status.PLACED) status = Status.PACKED; }
void ship()    { if (status == Status.PACKED) status = Status.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY; }
void deliver() { status = Status.DELIVERED; }                                 // no check: surely the driver knows
void cancel()  { if (status != Status.DELIVERED) status = Status.CANCELLED; }  // forgot: the van may have left
Kotlin
// Naive: each button guards only what its author thought of
fun pack()    { if (status == Status.PLACED) status = Status.PACKED }
fun ship()    { if (status == Status.PACKED) status = Status.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY }
fun deliver() { status = Status.DELIVERED }                                   // no check: surely the driver knows
fun cancel()  { if (status != Status.DELIVERED) status = Status.CANCELLED }    // forgot: the van may have left

OrderButtonsDemo, in the Try it, presses Pack, Ship, Cancel, Deliver, and then Pack once more by mistake:

pack     -> PACKED
ship     -> OUT_FOR_DELIVERY
cancel   -> CANCELLED
deliver  -> DELIVERED
pack     -> DELIVERED

The customer cancelled while the parcel was on the road, and the driver delivered it anyway. The shop now has a teapot that was cancelled and delivered, in that order. The last click did nothing at all, and nobody said so.

The cause isn't one careless line. The rules for an order live in four places, and each button knows a different part of them. A fifth button means remembering every rule again.

State is the pattern for this: an object's behavior depends on the state it's in, so each state should say which moves it allows. The 1994 book of design patterns gives each state its own class. Modern Java and Kotlin let us write it smaller. A state is where the order is in its life, holding exactly the data that state needs. An event is something that happens to the order, such as a button press. A transition function takes the current state and an event, and returns the next state. The states and events below are records, small classes that just hold their data, and each set is sealed: its interface lists every type allowed to implement it, so the compiler knows the whole set:

Java
sealed interface OrderState permits Placed, Packed, OutForDelivery, Delivered, Cancelled {}
record Placed(String orderNo) implements OrderState {}
record Packed(String orderNo, int parcels) implements OrderState {}
record OutForDelivery(String orderNo, int parcels, String courier) implements OrderState {}
record Delivered(String orderNo, String signedBy) implements OrderState {}
record Cancelled(String orderNo, String reason) implements OrderState {}

sealed interface OrderEvent permits Pack, Ship, Deliver, Cancel {}
record Pack(int parcels) implements OrderEvent {}
record Ship(String courier) implements OrderEvent {}
record Deliver(String signedBy) implements OrderEvent {}
record Cancel(String reason) implements OrderEvent {}

static OrderState transition(OrderState s, OrderEvent e) {
    return switch (s) {                                  // no default: a new state breaks the build
        case Placed p -> switch (e) {
            case Pack(var parcels) when parcels > 0 -> new Packed(p.orderNo(), parcels);
            case Cancel(var reason) -> new Cancelled(p.orderNo(), reason);
            default -> throw illegal(s, e);
        };
        case Packed(var no, var parcels) -> switch (e) {
            case Ship(var courier) -> new OutForDelivery(no, parcels, courier);
            case Cancel(var reason) -> new Cancelled(no, reason);
            default -> throw illegal(s, e);
        };
        case OutForDelivery o -> switch (e) {
            case Deliver(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Delivered(o.orderNo(), who);
            default -> throw illegal(s, e);              // Cancel lands here: the van has left
        };
        case Delivered d -> throw illegal(s, e);         // final
        case Cancelled c -> throw illegal(s, e);         // final
    };
}
Kotlin
sealed interface OrderState {
    data class Placed(val orderNo: String) : OrderState
    data class Packed(val orderNo: String, val parcels: Int) : OrderState
    data class OutForDelivery(val orderNo: String, val parcels: Int, val courier: String) : OrderState
    data class Delivered(val orderNo: String, val signedBy: String) : OrderState
    data class Cancelled(val orderNo: String, val reason: String) : OrderState
}
sealed interface OrderEvent {
    data class Pack(val parcels: Int) : OrderEvent
    data class Ship(val courier: String) : OrderEvent
    data class Deliver(val signedBy: String) : OrderEvent
    data class Cancel(val reason: String) : OrderEvent
}

fun transition(s: OrderState, e: OrderEvent): OrderState = when (s) {   // no else: a new state breaks the build
    is OrderState.Placed -> when (e) {
        is OrderEvent.Pack if e.parcels > 0 -> OrderState.Packed(s.orderNo, e.parcels)
        is OrderEvent.Cancel -> OrderState.Cancelled(s.orderNo, e.reason)
        else -> throw illegal(s, e)
    }
    is OrderState.Packed -> when (e) {
        is OrderEvent.Ship -> OrderState.OutForDelivery(s.orderNo, s.parcels, e.courier)
        is OrderEvent.Cancel -> OrderState.Cancelled(s.orderNo, e.reason)
        else -> throw illegal(s, e)
    }
    is OrderState.OutForDelivery -> when (e) {
        is OrderEvent.Deliver if e.signedBy.isNotBlank() -> OrderState.Delivered(s.orderNo, e.signedBy)
        else -> throw illegal(s, e)                                    // Cancel lands here: the van has left
    }
    is OrderState.Delivered, is OrderState.Cancelled -> throw illegal(s, e)    // final
}

Read it as a table. Each outer case is a state, each inner case is an event that state accepts, and everything else throws. A record pattern such as Packed(var no, var parcels) takes the record's fields out as it matches. A guard, the when parcels > 0 part, adds a condition: if it's false, the case doesn't match. Kotlin's guards in when (is Pack if ...) became stable in Kotlin 2.2.0.

Picture the order board in the back room. It has five columns, one per state, and a card for each order. A rule card pinned above the board says which moves are allowed. The transition function is that rule card, kept in one place and checked by the compiler. The picture breaks in a useful spot. On a real board, every card looks the same. In code, each column has its own kind of card: an OutForDelivery card has a space for the courier, and a Placed card has none, so a placed order can't carry a courier by mistake.

The function is pure: an old state and an event go in, a new state comes out, and nothing else is touched. You can test it without any fake objects, and replaying an order's history is one loop, as the lab's replay shows. Keep the side effects, such as booking the van, outside it: book first, then feed the answer in as an event.

Rules spread over buttons drift apart. Put them in one transition function, and let the buttons only send events.

One function holds the rules now. Next, we'll add a sixth state and let the compiler find every place it touches.

try.title: Press the buttons in the wrong order
steps: Read OrderButtonsDemo.java (or OrderButtonsDemo.kt). Predict the five lines it prints.
Run it with the command below.

Fix cancel so it refuses once the order has left: if (status == Status.PLACED || status == Status.PACKED) status = Status.CANCELLED; (the same line in Kotlin, without the semicolon). Predict the output and run it. Then ask: what is the customer who pressed Cancel told?

code.title: OrderButtonsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l09; /** Naive: an order with a status field, and four buttons that each check only what their author remembered. */ public class OrderButtonsDemo { enum Status { PLACED, PACKED, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, CANCELLED } static final class Order { final String orderNo; Status status = Status.PLACED; Order(String orderNo) { this.orderNo = orderNo; } void pack() { if (status == Status.PLACED) status = Status.PACKED; } void ship() { if (status == Status.PACKED) status = Status.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY; } void deliver() { status = Status.DELIVERED; // no check: surely the driver knows } void cancel() { if (status != Status.DELIVERED) status = Status.CANCELLED; // forgot: the van may have left } } public static void main(String[] args) { Order o = new Order("7781"); o.pack(); System.out.println("pack -> " + o.status); o.ship(); System.out.println("ship -> " + o.status); o.cancel(); // the customer presses Cancel; the van is on the road System.out.println("cancel -> " + o.status); o.deliver(); // the driver hands the parcel over anyway System.out.println("deliver -> " + o.status); o.pack(); // a stray click: nothing happens, and nobody says so System.out.println("pack -> " + o.status); } }

try.expect: PACKED, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, CANCELLED, DELIVERED, then DELIVERED again: a cancelled order was delivered, and the last Pack did nothing without a word. With the fix, the line reads cancel -> OUT_FOR_DELIVERY and the rest is right. But Cancel now fails silently too, so the customer is told nothing. One more if fixed one button, and the rules are still spread over four of them.

sections.h: Add a state, and let the compiler list every place it touches
sections.html:
Some deliveries fail because nobody is home. The shop decides to keep those parcels at the counter until the customer collects, so an order needs a sixth state, WaitingAtShop. Add the record to the sealed interface and build, before you write a single rule:

javac:   error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is WaitingAtShop' branch or an 'else' branch.

Every switch over the state type fails, and each error points at one place that needs a decision: the transition function, the label on the shop's screen, the count of orders on the evening report. A switch the compiler has checked against every subtype is called an exhaustive switch. The compiler, strict as ever, has written your to-do list. Work through it, and the feature is done when the build is green.

That only works if you leave room for it. A default (or else) on a switch over your own sealed type means "and anything else", and the compiler believes you: WaitingAtShop falls into the default without a word. The inner switches in transition do use default, on purpose. Most (state, event) pairs aren't allowed, and listing each one adds nothing. So the rule is narrower than "never write default": never write it on the side you expect to grow. States grow. The events one state accepts mostly don't.

A default on the switch over states hides every state you add later. Leave it off.

The check happens when the code is compiled, so a small gap is left for run time. The design notes for Java's pattern matching, by Brian Goetz and Gavin Bierman, call it the remainder: the values a checked switch can still meet. One is null, and a switch on a null state throws NullPointerException. The other is a subtype (a type that implements the sealed interface) added after the switch was compiled, in a separately compiled jar (a file of compiled classes). Java throws MatchException for it, and Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. You don't write code for those cases, but a program that mixes old and new jars can meet them.

State looks a lot like Strategy, from Strategy and Template Method: an object holds a value, and behavior depends on it. The difference is who chooses. The shopkeeper picks a strategy, such as "cheapest courier", and it stays put. A state machine picks its own next state as events arrive.

A state machine decides what one order may do. Next, we'll look at a request that several people could answer.

try.title: Walk a return, then add a state
steps: Open ReturnStateDemo.java (or .kt). A customer returns a teapot, and the return has a life of its own, with the same shape as an order. Predict the five lines it prints, then run it.
Change the approver from "dana" to " " (a blank name). Predict where the program stops and what it prints, run it, then change it back.

Add a state. Java: add record OnHold(String id, String item) implements ReturnState {} and add OnHold to the permits list. Kotlin: add data class OnHold(val id: String, val item: String) : ReturnState inside the sealed interface. Before you build with the demo command, predict how many errors you'll get, and where.
Fix them: in next, a return on hold accepts nothing yet (throw illegal(s, e)); in label, return "on hold". Build again, then remove OnHold.

code.title: ReturnStateDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l09; import java.util.List; /** A customer's return as a state machine: states and events are data, the rules are one pure function. */ public class ReturnStateDemo { sealed interface ReturnState permits Requested, Approved, Collected, BackOnShelf, Binned {} record Requested(String id, String item) implements ReturnState {} record Approved(String id, String item, String approver) implements ReturnState {} record Collected(String id, String item, String label) implements ReturnState {} record BackOnShelf(String id, String item) implements ReturnState {} record Binned(String id, String reason) implements ReturnState {} sealed interface ReturnEvent permits Approve, Collect, PutBack, Damaged {} record Approve(String approver) implements ReturnEvent {} record Collect(String label) implements ReturnEvent {} record PutBack() implements ReturnEvent {} record Damaged(String reason) implements ReturnEvent {} static ReturnState next(ReturnState s, ReturnEvent e) { return switch (s) { // no default: a new state breaks the build case Requested(var id, var item) -> switch (e) { case Approve(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Approved(id, item, who); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Approved(var id, var item, var who) -> switch (e) { case Collect(var label) -> new Collected(id, item, label); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Collected(var id, var item, var label) -> switch (e) { case PutBack() -> new BackOnShelf(id, item); case Damaged(var reason) -> new Binned(id, reason); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case BackOnShelf done -> throw illegal(s, e); // final case Binned done -> throw illegal(s, e); // final }; } // a second switch over the same states: the label on the shop's screen static String label(ReturnState s) { return switch (s) { case Requested r -> "waiting for approval"; case Approved a -> "approved by " + a.approver(); case Collected c -> "collected, label " + c.label(); case BackOnShelf b -> b.item() + " is back on the shelf"; case Binned b -> "binned: " + b.reason(); }; } static IllegalStateException illegal(ReturnState s, ReturnEvent e) { return new IllegalStateException(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " not allowed in " + s.getClass().getSimpleName()); } public static void main(String[] args) { ReturnState s = new Requested("rt-31", "teapot"); System.out.println(label(s)); for (ReturnEvent e : List.of(new Approve("dana"), new Collect("RT-0091"), new PutBack())) { s = next(s, e); System.out.println(label(s)); } try { next(new Requested("rt-32", "kettle"), new Collect("RT-0092")); } catch (IllegalStateException ex) { System.out.println("rejected: " + ex.getMessage()); } } }

id: String, val item: String) : ReturnState data class Approved(val id: String, val item: String, val approver: String) : ReturnState data class Collected(val id: String, val item: String, val label: String) : ReturnState data class BackOnShelf(val id: String, val item: String) : ReturnState data class Binned(val id: String, val reason: String) : ReturnState } sealed interface ReturnEvent { data class Approve(val approver: String) : ReturnEvent data class Collect(val label: String) : ReturnEvent data object PutBack : ReturnEvent data class Damaged(val reason: String) : ReturnEvent } private fun next(s: ReturnState, e: ReturnEvent): ReturnState = when (s) { // no else: a new state breaks the build is ReturnState.Requested -> when (e) { is ReturnEvent.Approve if e.approver.isNotBlank() -> ReturnState.Approved(s.id, s.item, e.approver) else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is ReturnState.Approved -> when (e) { is ReturnEvent.Collect -> ReturnState.Collected(s.id, s.item, e.label) else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is ReturnState.Collected -> when (e) { ReturnEvent.PutBack -> ReturnState.BackOnShelf(s.id, s.item) is ReturnEvent.Damaged -> ReturnState.Binned(s.id, e.reason) else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is ReturnState.BackOnShelf, is ReturnState.Binned -> throw illegal(s, e) // final } // a second when over the same states: the label on the shop's screen private fun label(s: ReturnState): String = when (s) { is ReturnState.Requested -> "waiting for approval" is ReturnState.Approved -> "approved by ${s.approver}" is ReturnState.Collected -> "collected, label ${s.label}" is ReturnState.BackOnShelf -> "${s.item} is back on the shelf" is ReturnState.Binned -> "binned: ${s.reason}" } private fun illegal(s: ReturnState, e: ReturnEvent) = IllegalStateException("${e::class.simpleName} not allowed in ${s::class.simpleName}") fun main() { var s: ReturnState = ReturnState.Requested("rt-31", "teapot") println(label(s)) for (e in listOf(ReturnEvent.Approve("dana"), ReturnEvent.Collect("RT-0091"), ReturnEvent.PutBack)) { s = next(s, e) println(label(s)) } try { next(ReturnState.Requested("rt-32", "kettle"), ReturnEvent.Collect("RT-0092")) } catch (ex: IllegalStateException) { println("rejected: ${ex.message}") } }

try.expect: waiting for approval, approved by dana, collected, label RT-0091, teapot is back on the shelf, then rejected: Collect not allowed in Requested, because a return must be approved before anyone collects it. With a blank approver, the guard when !who.isBlank() fails, the event falls to the inner default, and the program stops at the first event with IllegalStateException: Approve not allowed in Requested: the guard is part of the rule. Adding OnHold gives two errors, one per switch over the state, in next and in label. javac says the switch expression does not cover all possible input values twice, and kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is OnHold' branch or an 'else' branch. twice. Two new branches make the build green: the compiler's list was complete.

sections.h: Chain of Responsibility: answer the complaint, or pass it on
sections.html:
A customer comes to the counter: the teapot from the gift box arrived cracked. The shop assistant can sort out anything worth up to 5.00 herself, from the shelf. Anything bigger goes to the manager, who can sort out up to 50.00. The rest goes to head office, which answers everything, eventually. Nobody needs to know who sits further down the line. Each person either answers or passes the complaint on.

That is Chain of Responsibility: a request travels along a list of handlers, and each handler either answers it or passes it to the next one. In code, each link is a function of the complaint and next, the rest of the chain:

Java
Handler assistant = (c, next) -> c.worthCents() <= 500
        ? new Reply("assistant", "sorted")              // answer now: the rest never runs
        : next.passOn(c);                                // pass it on

Handler book = (c, next) -> {
    Reply r = next.passOn(c);                            // what follows runs on the way back
    System.out.println("  book: " + c.orderNo() + " " + c.about() + " -> " + r.from());
    return r;
};

Chain desk = chain(List.of(book, receipt, oncePerOrder, assistant, manager), headOffice);
Kotlin
val assistant = Handler { c, next ->
    if (c.worthCents <= 500) Reply("assistant", "sorted")   // answer now: the rest never runs
    else next(c)                                             // pass it on
}

val book = Handler { c, next ->
    next(c).also { println("  book: ${c.orderNo} ${c.about} -> ${it.from}") }   // runs on the way back
}

val shopDesk = desk(listOf(book, receipt, oncePerOrder, assistant, manager), headOffice)

Each Complaint record says which order it's about, what went wrong, what putting it right is worth in cents, and whether the customer brought the receipt. receipt turns away a complaint without one, and oncePerOrder turns away a second complaint about an order that's already been sorted.

The complaints book on the counter is the first link, and it shows the shape of every handler. Code before next runs on the way in, code after it runs on the way back with the reply, and not calling next at all ends the trip early. So the book sees every complaint and every answer, while the receipt check can turn a customer away before the assistant even looks.

The 1994 book links handler objects with a setNext() method. You don't need that. A list of functions and a fold make the chain. A fold walks a list and builds one result from it, step by step: here, start from the last stop and wrap it in each handler, from the last one to the first. The result can't change, so one desk can serve every complaint on every thread (a path of work that runs side by side with others). The lab's ComplaintDesk.build copies the list it's given for the same reason: a later edit to the caller's list must not change a chain that's already in use.

The picture breaks on the way back. In the shop, an assistant who passes a complaint to the manager may never hear how it ended. In code, the reply travels back through every link that passed it on, and each one can still read it, write it down or change it. The figure shows both directions.

The chain is short and easy to build. Next, we'll see the four ways it goes wrong.

try.title: Swap two handlers
steps: Read ComplaintDeskDemo.java (or .kt). The third complaint has no receipt; the fourth is the same customer coming back with it. Predict the four replies and the complaints sorted count.
Run it with the command below.
Swap receipt and oncePerOrder in the list, so it reads book, oncePerOrder, receipt, assistant, manager. Predict the last reply and the count, then run.

code.title: ComplaintDeskDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l09; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** A complaint passes along the shop's desk: each handler answers it or passes it on. The order of the list is behavior. */ public class ComplaintDeskDemo { record Complaint(String orderNo, String about, int worthCents, boolean hasReceipt) {} record Reply(String from, String says) {} interface Chain { Reply passOn(Complaint c); } interface Handler { Reply handle(Complaint c, Chain next); } // fold the handlers into one chain, from the last to the first static Chain chain(List<Handler> handlers, Chain lastStop) { Chain next = lastStop; for (int i = handlers.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Handler h = handlers.get(i); Chain rest = next; next = c -> h.handle(c, rest); } return next; } static int sorted = 0; static Reply sort(String who) { sorted++; return new Reply(who, "sorted"); } public static void main(String[] args) { Set<String> handled = new HashSet<>(); Handler book = (c, next) -> { Reply r = next.passOn(c); // in: nothing; out: write it in the book System.out.println(" book: " + c.orderNo() + " " + c.about() + " -> " + r.from()); return r; }; Handler receipt = (c, next) -> c.hasReceipt() ? next.passOn(c) : new Reply("assistant", "please bring the receipt"); // answer now: the rest never runs Handler oncePerOrder = (c, next) -> handled.add(c.orderNo()) ? next.passOn(c) : new Reply("assistant", "we sorted this one already"); Handler assistant = (c, next) -> c.worthCents() <= 500 ? sort("assistant") : next.passOn(c); Handler manager = (c, next) -> c.worthCents() <= 5_000 ? sort("manager") : next.passOn(c); Chain headOffice = c -> sort("head office"); // the last stop answers everything Chain desk = chain(List.of(book, receipt, oncePerOrder, assistant, manager), headOffice); for (Complaint c : List.of( new Complaint("7781", "cracked teapot", 1_800, true), new Complaint("7781", "cracked teapot", 1_800, true), // the same complaint again new Complaint("7782", "stale bread", 250, false), // receipt left at home new Complaint("7782", "stale bread", 250, true))) { // back with the receipt Reply r = desk.passOn(c); System.out.println(r.from() + ": " + r.says()); } System.out.println("complaints sorted: " + sorted); } }

alt.title: ComplaintDeskDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l09 // A complaint passes along the shop's desk: each handler answers it or passes it on. The order of the list is behavior. data class Complaint(val orderNo: String, val about: String, val worthCents: Int, val hasReceipt: Boolean) data class Reply(val from: String, val says: String) fun interface Handler { fun handle(c: Complaint, next: (Complaint) -> Reply): Reply } // fold the handlers into one function, from the last to the first fun desk(handlers: List<Handler>, lastStop: (Complaint) -> Reply): (Complaint) -> Reply = handlers.foldRight(lastStop) { h, next -> { c -> h.handle(c, next) } } fun main() { var sorted = 0 fun sort(who: String): Reply { sorted++; return Reply(who, "sorted") } val handled = mutableSetOf<String>() val book = Handler { c, next -> next(c).also { println(" book: ${c.orderNo} ${c.about} -> ${it.from}") } // in: nothing; out: write it in the book } val receipt = Handler { c, next -> if (c.hasReceipt) next(c) else Reply("assistant", "please bring the receipt") // answer now: the rest never runs } val oncePerOrder = Handler { c, next -> if (handled.add(c.orderNo)) next(c) else Reply("assistant", "we sorted this one already") } val assistant = Handler { c, next -> if (c.worthCents <= 500) sort("assistant") else next(c) } val manager = Handler { c, next -> if (c.worthCents <= 5_000) sort("manager") else next(c) } val headOffice = { _: Complaint -> sort("head office") } // the last stop answers everything val shopDesk = desk(listOf(book, receipt, oncePerOrder, assistant, manager), headOffice) for (c in listOf( Complaint("7781", "cracked teapot", 1_800, true), Complaint("7781", "cracked teapot", 1_800, true), // the same complaint again Complaint("7782", "stale bread", 250, false), // receipt left at home Complaint("7782", "stale bread", 250, true), // back with the receipt )) { val r = shopDesk(c) println("${r.from}: ${r.says}") } println("complaints sorted: $sorted") }

try.expect: In order: manager: sorted (the cracked teapot is worth 18.00, too much for the assistant), assistant: we sorted this one already, assistant: please bring the receipt, assistant: sorted, and complaints sorted: 2. The book writes a line for every complaint, the turned-away ones included. After the swap, the complaint without a receipt is marked as handled before the receipt check turns it away, so the customer who comes back with the receipt hears we sorted this one already, and the count drops to 1. Nobody sorted out the stale bread.

video.title: A request runs along a chain of checks until one answers, and the order of the list is behavior; then a payment's state decides which event is legal

sections.h: Four ways a chain of handlers goes wrong
sections.html:
Chains fail in four ways, and each one looks like a bug somewhere else.

The order is wrong. Handlers run in list order, so the order of the list is behavior. Put the once-per-order check before the receipt check, as the Try it did, and a customer turned away for a missing receipt has already used up their one complaint. Put the book after the receipt check, and turned-away customers never reach the book. Pin the order with a test.

A handler forgets next. A handler that neither answers nor calls next has nothing to return. In Java it's tempting to return null, and the complaint simply disappears, until a caller trips over the null with a NullPointerException. Every path through a handler must either call next or return a real reply.

A handler calls next twice. A "try again" step that wraps next.passOn(c) near the front of the chain repeats everything after it. If the assistant's step posts a new teapot, two teapots go out. Put a retry as close as possible to the one call it repeats, never around the rest of the chain.

A later handler throws an exception. Then the code after next.passOn(c) in the earlier handlers never runs, so the book never writes its line. Anything that must happen on the way back, such as the book's line or stopping a timer, belongs in a finally block.

Every path through a handler answers or calls next, exactly once. Put the work for the way back in finally.

Check yourself. In the desk from the last section, the manager's step throws for one complaint. Does that complaint get a line in the book, which is first in the list? (No. The book writes its line after next.passOn(c) returns, and that call never returns. Wrap it in try/finally, write the line in the finally, and the complaint shows up in the book, with the exception still on its way out.)

aside.title: Where will I meet this chain in real programs?
aside.html: Almost every web framework has one. A Java web server passes each request through a list of servlet filters before your code sees it: each Filter gets the request and a FilterChain, and calls chain.doFilter(request, response) to pass it on. OkHttp, a widely used library for making web requests, has interceptors that call chain.proceed(request) in the same way. Frameworks also put interceptors around your own methods, for jobs such as opening a database transaction, and sort them by a priority number. When a filter seems not to run, check its place in the order before you read its code.

compare.title: Building the chain: an index walker and a fold

java.title: RealChain.java
java.html: // OkHttp's shape: a chain object that can't change and knows its position interface Chain { Reply passOn(Complaint c); } interface Handler { Reply handle(Complaint c, Chain next); } record RealChain(List<Handler> handlers, int index, Function<Complaint, Reply> lastStop) implements Chain { RealChain { handlers = List.copyOf(handlers); // cheap after the first time: copyOf keeps an unmodifiable list } public Reply passOn(Complaint c) { if (index == handlers.size()) return lastStop.apply(c); // past the last link return handlers.get(index).handle(c, new RealChain(handlers, index + 1, lastStop)); } } Chain desk = new RealChain(List.of(book, receipt, assistant), 0, headOffice);

kotlin.title: Desk.kt
kotlin.html: // a function type replaces the Chain interface: the chain is just (Complaint) -> Reply fun interface Handler { fun handle(c: Complaint, next: (Complaint) -> Reply): Reply } fun desk(handlers: List<Handler>, lastStop: (Complaint) -> Reply): (Complaint) -> Reply = handlers.foldRight(lastStop) { h, next -> { c -> h.handle(c, next) } } // wrap from the last to the first val shopDesk = desk(listOf(book, receipt, assistant), headOffice)

compare.note: Both call the handlers in the same order, and neither can change after it's built. The Java record walks an index and creates a small chain object per step, for every complaint. That object is a natural place to carry more, which is why OkHttp (a library for making web requests) builds its real chain this way and lets it carry the call and its timeouts. The Kotlin fold builds the nested functions once, and next is a plain function, so no Chain interface is needed. Java can fold too, with a loop from the last handler to the first, as the lab's ComplaintDesk.build does. What both languages make unnecessary is the 1994 book's handler base class, with a setNext() link that anyone can change.

worked.title: Add a "nobody home" state to an order's life

steps.say: Some deliveries fail because nobody is home. The shop keeps those parcels at the counter: the customer can collect and sign there, or ask for a second try. Start with data only: one new state and one new event.
steps.code: sealed interface OrderState permits Placed, Packed, OutForDelivery, Delivered, Cancelled, WaitingAtShop {} record WaitingAtShop(String orderNo, int parcels) implements OrderState {} // 1. the new state sealed interface OrderEvent permits Pack, Ship, Deliver, Cancel, NobodyHome {} record NobodyHome() implements OrderEvent {} // 2. the new event

alt.html: sealed interface OrderState { // ...the five existing states, plus: data class WaitingAtShop(val orderNo: String, val parcels: Int) : OrderState // 1. the new state } sealed interface OrderEvent { // ...the four existing events, plus: data object NobodyHome : OrderEvent // 2. the new event }

steps.say: Compile before writing any rule. Every switch over OrderState fails; in a bigger program, the list might look like this. Count the errors: that's the size of the feature. Why does none of the inner switches over events fail?
steps.code:
OrderLife.java:41: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
ScreenLabels.java:12: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
EveningReport.java:27: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values

(kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is WaitingAtShop' branch or an 'else' branch.)

steps.say: The inner switches have a default, so the new event simply isn't allowed in the old states until you say otherwise. Now write the rules. Note the choice in step 5: a waiting parcel is back in the shop, so cancelling is fine again.
steps.code: case OutForDelivery o -> switch (e) { case Deliver(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Delivered(o.orderNo(), who); case NobodyHome() -> new WaitingAtShop(o.orderNo(), o.parcels()); // 3. the parcel comes back default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case WaitingAtShop(var no, var parcels) -> switch (e) { case Ship(var courier) -> new OutForDelivery(no, parcels, courier); // 4. a second try case Deliver(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Delivered(no, who); // or collected at the counter case Cancel(var reason) -> new Cancelled(no, reason); // 5. it's in the shop: cancel is fine default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Delivered d -> throw illegal(s, e); case Cancelled c -> throw illegal(s, e);

alt.html: is OrderState.OutForDelivery -> when (e) { is OrderEvent.Deliver if e.signedBy.isNotBlank() -> OrderState.Delivered(s.orderNo, e.signedBy) OrderEvent.NobodyHome -> OrderState.WaitingAtShop(s.orderNo, s.parcels) // 3. the parcel comes back else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is OrderState.WaitingAtShop -> when (e) { is OrderEvent.Ship -> OrderState.OutForDelivery(s.orderNo, s.parcels, e.courier) // 4. a second try is OrderEvent.Deliver if e.signedBy.isNotBlank() -> OrderState.Delivered(s.orderNo, e.signedBy) // or collected is OrderEvent.Cancel -> OrderState.Cancelled(s.orderNo, e.reason) // 5. it's in the shop: cancel is fine else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is OrderState.Delivered, is OrderState.Cancelled -> throw illegal(s, e)

steps.say: Fix the screen label and the evening report the same way, then pin the new paths in tests. Because transition is pure, a whole failed delivery is one replay call, with no courier and no database.
steps.code: @Test void nobodyHomeThenCollectedAtTheCounter() { var events = List.<OrderEvent>of(new Pack(1), new Ship("Big Blue Vans"), new NobodyHome(), new Deliver("Ben")); assertThat(replay("7790", events)).isEqualTo(new Delivered("7790", "Ben")); } @Test void cancelIsAllowedAgainOnceTheParcelIsBack() { assertThat(transition(new WaitingAtShop("7790", 1), new Cancel("moved away"))) .isEqualTo(new Cancelled("7790", "moved away")); }

alt.html: @Test fun `nobody home, then collected at the counter`() { val events = listOf(OrderEvent.Pack(1), OrderEvent.Ship("Big Blue Vans"), OrderEvent.NobodyHome, OrderEvent.Deliver("Ben")) val end: OrderState = events.fold(OrderState.Placed("7790"), ::transition) assertThat(end).isEqualTo(OrderState.Delivered("7790", "Ben")) } @Test fun `cancel is allowed again once the parcel is back`() { assertThat(transition(OrderState.WaitingAtShop("7790", 1), OrderEvent.Cancel("moved away"))) .isEqualTo(OrderState.Cancelled("7790", "moved away")) }

lab.title: An order's life and a complaint desk
steps: Read the table in the Javadoc of OrderLife, and the given illegal and replay methods. Run the tests: all ten fail.
Write transition as a switch expression over the state with no default, and a switch over the event inside each state's case. Use record patterns, and when guards for the parcel and signature rules.
In ComplaintDesk, write build: copy the list, start from Chain next = lastStop::apply, and loop from the last handler to the first, wrapping next each time.
Write upTo and lateDelivery as one-line lambdas (c, next) -> ....
Run the tests until all ten pass. Then add a WaitingAtShop record to OrderState (and to permits), build, read the error, and remove it.
hints: In a switch expression, case Delivered d -> throw illegal(s, e); is a complete case: a throw is allowed where a value is expected.
A lambda can only use local variables that never change after they're set, so copy the loop's values first: Handler handler = copy.get(i); Chain rest = next; next = c -> handler.handle(c, rest);.
case Packed(var no, var parcels) -> switch (e) { case Ship(var courier) -> new OutForDelivery(no, parcels, courier); ... } takes the fields out and builds the next state in one line.

drill.title: Fold a chain from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write chain(handlers, lastStop), which folds a list of handlers into one function, where each handler gets the complaint and next. Then answer: for [a, b, c], in what order do they run on the way in, and on the way back?

answer.html: static Chain chain(List<Handler> handlers, Chain lastStop) { Chain next = lastStop; for (int i = handlers.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { // wrap from the last to the first Handler h = handlers.get(i); Chain rest = next; next = c -> h.handle(c, rest); } return next; } // on the way in: a, b, c, then the last stop; on the way back: c, b, a

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: fun desk(handlers: List<Handler>, lastStop: (Complaint) -> Reply): (Complaint) -> Reply = handlers.foldRight(lastStop) { h, next -> { c -> h.handle(c, next) } } // wrap from the last to the first // on the way in: a, b, c, then the last stop; on the way back: c, b, a

recap: State: model a lifecycle as sealed states, sealed events and one pure transition function. Record patterns and guards (when, or if in Kotlin 2.2 and later) state each rule in one line.
No default on the switch over states: a new state then fails to compile at every place that needs a rule. A default on the inner switch over events is fine, because most pairs aren't allowed.
A pure transition function turns history into a loop: replaying the events rebuilds the state, and tests need no fake objects.
Chain of Responsibility: each handler answers now or calls next. Code before next runs on the way in, code after it on the way back.
Chains break on order, a forgotten next, a doubled next and exceptions. Pin the order in a test, and put the work for the way back in finally.

The limit: the compiler checks only code compiled together. null and a subtype from a separately compiled jar still reach a switch at run time, as NullPointerException, MatchException (Java) or NoWhenBranchMatchedException (Kotlin).

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why transition has no default on its outer switch but does have one on each inner switch, and what the compiler gives you when someone adds a WaitingAtShop state.
explain.answer: The outer switch is over states, and states are what we expect to add: waiting at the shop, on hold, split into two parcels. With no default, the compiler knows the switch must cover every permitted state, so adding WaitingAtShop makes every switch over OrderState in the program fail to compile. Those errors are the list of places that need a decision, and the feature is finished when the build is green. The inner switches are over the events one state accepts. Most events aren't allowed in most states, and a new event usually matters in only one or two of them, so a default that throws "not allowed" is the honest rule there. A default on the outer switch would swallow the new state without a word, and waiting orders would reject every event when the program runs.

deeper.html:
Pattern matching for switch (JEP 441) and record patterns (JEP 440) both became final in JDK 21, so everything in this lesson compiles with --release 21 and no preview flags. In Kotlin, the subclasses of a sealed type must live in the same package and module as the type itself, and guards in when with a subject became stable in 2.2.0.

Keeping the transition pure doesn't mean the order does nothing. A common shape returns the next state together with a list of things to do, such as "book the van", "text the customer" or "print the label", written as sealed records. A thin outer layer does them and feeds the results back in as events. Tests then check the returned list, with no fake courier at all.

Event sourcing takes replay to its end: store the events, not the state, and compute the state with a loop over them. A long history gets slow to replay, so programs that work this way save a snapshot every few hundred events and replay only what came after it. That snapshot is a memento, from the next lesson, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento.

Chains of handlers also wrap single methods, not only whole requests. Many frameworks let you put an interceptor around a method: it gets an object describing the call and calls proceed() to go on to the next interceptor or the method itself. Those interceptors live in proxies, so the rules from Decorator and Proxy apply to them: a method that calls another method on this skips them.
